mcqs.question: A style change invalidates the Paint stage of the rendering pipeline. Which stages run?
options: Paint and Composite — layout is skipped, but everything downstream of paint still runs
Paint only — the browser can hand the existing frame to the screen unchanged
Style, Layout, Paint, and Composite — the pipeline always runs from the start
Paint and Layout — the browser re-measures boxes to know what area to redraw
mcqs.explanation: The pipeline is entered at the invalidated stage and every stage after it must re-run, so a paint invalidation costs paint plus composite and skips layout. It cannot stop at paint, because painted pixels still have to be assembled into a frame, and it never runs layout afterwards — layout precedes paint in the sequence.

mcqs.question: Why can changing the width of a single element cost far more than the work of measuring that one element?
options: Because the browser has to recompute every CSS selector match in the document
Because width changes force the GPU to discard and recreate all compositor layers
Because layout is relational — in normal flow the element's siblings and ancestors may shift, so many nodes need re-measuring
Because the browser cannot cache computed styles for elements whose width is dynamic
mcqs.explanation: In normal document flow a box's position depends on the boxes around it, so widening one element can push everything after it and force a re-measure across a large part of the tree. Selector matching is the earlier Style stage and is not what makes reflow expensive, and layer recreation is a compositing concern unrelated to a width change.

mcqs.question: A long-running script blocks the main thread for 200ms. What happens to a running CSS `transform` animation on a promoted element versus a `left` animation?
options: Both freeze, because all CSS animations are driven by the main thread's frame loop
The `transform` animation keeps running on the compositor thread while the `left` animation freezes
Both keep running, because CSS animations never depend on JavaScript
The `transform` animation freezes but resumes at the correct position, while the `left` animation restarts
mcqs.explanation: A composited transform or opacity animation can be handed to the compositor thread, so it keeps advancing even while the main thread is blocked; a `left` animation needs main-thread layout every frame and stops dead. This off-main-thread property, not just the raw per-frame cost, is usually why the transform version feels dramatically smoother in production.

mcqs.question: You need to hide an element and its space should collapse so following content moves up. What is the performance consequence?
options: None — hiding an element never triggers layout because nothing new is drawn
Only a repaint, since the element's pixels are cleared but geometry is untouched
A composite-only change, because hiding is equivalent to setting opacity to zero
A reflow, because removing the box from flow changes the geometry of everything after it
mcqs.explanation: Collapsing the space means using `display: none`, which takes the box out of flow so following content has to be re-laid-out — a full reflow plus paint and composite. `visibility: hidden` would be repaint-only, but it deliberately keeps the box's space, which is not what this requirement asks for.

mcqs.question: On a 60Hz display, a frame's work takes 17ms instead of the 16.7ms budget. What does the user see?
options: A frame rendered about 2% later, which is imperceptible
The animation smoothly slows to roughly 59fps
A visible stutter — the frame misses vsync entirely, so the previous frame stays on screen for 33ms
Nothing, because the browser interpolates the missing frame on the GPU
mcqs.explanation: Frame delivery is tied to vsync, so being even slightly over budget means the frame is not ready in time and the previous one is held for another full refresh interval — a 33ms hold that reads as a jump. The cost is a cliff, not a proportional slowdown, which is why 'just a little over budget' still looks broken.

mcqs.question: A colleague says a hover effect is 'GPU accelerated' so it can't be the source of jank. Which single DevTools check most directly settles it?
options: Run Lighthouse and check the Performance score before and after removing the effect
Turn on Paint flashing in the Rendering tab and watch whether regions highlight green while hovering
Check the Network panel for how long the stylesheet takes to download
Read the computed styles panel to confirm which properties the transition targets
mcqs.explanation: Paint flashing highlights every repainted region in real time, so if areas light up on each frame of the hover, the effect is provably not composite-only regardless of what the CSS looks like. Lighthouse scores load-time metrics and won't isolate a hover interaction, and reading the computed styles tells you intent rather than what the browser actually did.
